title: Median of two sorted arrays
sub: Binary search over the cut position, not the value: the correctness condition, sentinels at the edges and O(log min(m, n))
cards/0/body:
Median of Two Sorted Arrays (LeetCode #4, Hard). You get two sorted arrays: a of length m and b of length n, 0 ≤ m, n ≤ 1000, m + n ≥ 1. Return the median of their union as a double — in O(log(m + n)).

The median is the middle of a sorted list: for an odd length the middle element, for an even length the average of the two middle ones. [1, 3] and [2] → 2; [1, 2] and [3, 4] → (2 + 3) / 2 = 2.5.

Signals: both arrays are sorted, and the logarithmic requirement rules out even walking through them. So it is binary search — but not over values. We will search for the cut position.

This is the best-known Hard binary search problem. It is given to see how a candidate states the correctness condition and keeps the bounds straight; starting with the naive solution and naming its cost honestly is fine.
cards/1/title: Naive: merge up to the middle
cards/1/body:
Merge the arrays as in merge sort and take the middle: O(m + n) time and memory. You can do it without memory: walk two pointers only up to the middle, remembering the last two numbers taken.

With m + n ≤ 2000 this is instant, but the problem asks for O(log(m + n)) — and this is exactly where the interviewer expects the key idea. Name the merge anyway: it is your baseline and the reference you check the fast solution against on random tests.
cards/2/q: Merging with two pointers up to the middle. What is its complexity, and why is that a problem here?
cards/2/options/0: O(m + n) time, O(1) memory — while the problem asks for O(log(m + n))
cards/2/options/1: O((m + n) log(m + n)): it is essentially a sort
cards/2/options/2: O(log(m + n)): the pointers only cover half
cards/2/options/3: O(m · n): every element is compared with every other
cards/2/explain: There are (m + n) / 2 + 1 steps, and half is still linear work: the constant 1/2 is dropped in O. Memory is two pointers and two numbers. It works and passes the tests, but the logarithmic requirement says plainly: you may not look at every element up to the middle.
cards/2/wrong/1: There is no sorting: the arrays are already sorted, and merging is a single pass.
cards/2/wrong/2: Covering half is (m + n) / 2 steps, i.e. O(m + n). A logarithm is when every step discards half of what is left.
cards/2/wrong/3: Each step compares only the two current elements, one from each array.
cards/3/body:
The median splits the union into a left and a right part, with everything on the left ≤ everything on the right. Let the left part hold half = (m + n + 1) / 2 numbers — one more than the right when the total is odd. If we take the first i numbers of a, we must take j = half − i from b. Only i needs choosing — from 0 to m.

The cut is correct if everything on the left is no greater than everything on the right. Each array is already in order internally, so two cross comparisons are enough: a[i − 1] ≤ b[j] and b[j − 1] ≤ a[i]. Then the median is max(a[i − 1], b[j − 1]) for an odd total and the average of that maximum and min(a[i], b[j]) for an even one. Divide by 2.0: int / int in C# drops the fractional part.

Which way to move. If a[i − 1] > b[j], too much was taken from a — decrease i. If b[j − 1] > a[i], too little — increase it. As i grows, the edge a[i − 1] grows and b[j] shrinks, so “too much” is monotonic — that is a binary search over i on [0, m].

Sentinels. With i = 0 nothing from a is on the left — treat a[i − 1] = −∞, i.e. int.MinValue; with i = m nothing is on the right — a[i] = +∞, int.MaxValue. The same for b. The edges need no separate branches.

Why the shorter array. j = half − i must lie in [0, n] for every i in [0, m], and that is guaranteed only when m ≤ n. So if a is longer, swap the arrays. Hence the complexity — O(log min(m, n)).
cards/3/flow/0: i from a, j = half − i from b
cards/3/flow/1: a[i − 1] > b[j] → took too many: hi = i − 1
cards/3/flow/2: b[j − 1] > a[i] → took too few: lo = i + 1
cards/3/flow/3: otherwise the cut is correct → median from the edges
cards/4/q: Build the solution with the cut.
cards/4/explain: The left part must hold half numbers: take half − i from b. To the right of the cut a is empty when i = m — the +∞ sentinel, int.MaxValue. a[i − 1] > b[j] means too many were taken from a: hi = i − 1. With an odd total the extra element is on the left, and it is the median: the largest of the left edges. (lo + hi) / 2 cannot overflow here: hi ≤ m ≤ 1000.
cards/5/task: a = [22, 35, 38, 39], b = [1, 2, 4, 25, 29, 34]: 10 numbers in total, 5 must end up on the left. Step through the trace; the rig will stop twice.
cards/5/goal/asks/0/q: i = 2 took too many: a[1] = 35 > b[3] = 25, so hi = 1. The candidates for i are [0..1]. What is the next cut?
cards/5/goal/asks/0/explain: i = (0 + 1) / 2 = 0 — integer division rounds down — and j = 5 − 0 = 5. Nothing from a is on the left, so the left edge of a is the −∞ sentinel (int.MinValue): an empty left part needs no special handling. Next it turns out that b[4] = 29 > a[0] = 22 — now too few were taken from a, and i moves right.
cards/5/goal/asks/1/q: The cut i = 1, j = 4 is correct: on the left 22 and 1, 2, 4, 25; on the right 35, 38, 39 and 29, 34. What is the median?
cards/5/goal/asks/1/explain: 10 in total — even: the average of the largest on the left and the smallest on the right. max(22, 25) = 25, min(35, 29) = 29, (25 + 29) / 2.0 = 27. 28.5 is (22 + 35) / 2: the edges of one array, not of the union.
cards/6/q: The function returns double, yet on a = [1, 2], b = [3, 4] it gives 2 instead of 2.5. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/6/explain: (2 + 3) / 2 divides an int by an int, the result is 2, and only then does it become the double 2.0. It needs / 2.0 so the division happens in double. The cut itself is found correctly — i = 2, j = 0 — the bug is only in the final arithmetic.
cards/7/title: Edge cases and the k-th element
cards/7/body:
An empty array. If a is empty, m = 0: one iteration with i = 0, both edges of a are sentinels, and the median comes from b. No separate branch needed.
Sentinels never reach the answer. The left part holds half ≥ 1 numbers, so at least one of a[i − 1] and b[j − 1] is real — and so is the maximum. With an even total the right part also has at least one number — the minimum is real.
Without the swap, when m > n there is some i with j = half − i falls outside [0, n], and the access b[j] or b[j − 1] goes out of bounds.
Duplicates are fine: the conditions are non-strict, ≤.

The k-th smallest element of two arrays generalises this: the same cut, only with k numbers on the left, and i restricted so that j = k − i stays within [0, n]. The answer is the largest of the left edges.

The median of a stream is a different problem: numbers arrive one at a time, and the median is needed after each. That takes two heaps (the heaps unit), not binary search.
cards/8/q: What is true about the solution with the cut? Select all.
cards/8/options/0: The search runs over the shorter array, hence O(log min(m, n))
cards/8/options/1: Without swapping the arrays, j can become negative
cards/8/options/2: The int.MinValue and int.MaxValue sentinels never end up in the answer
cards/8/options/3: The solution is correct only if all numbers are distinct
cards/8/options/4: The median of the union always equals the average of the two arrays’ medians
cards/8/explain: The search over i on [0, m] with m ≤ n gives a logarithm of the shorter length, and j = half − i stays in [0, n]; without the swap, when m > n, j goes negative. There is always a real number on the left, and with an even total on the right as well — so sentinels never reach the answer. The conditions are non-strict, duplicates are fine. Averaging medians does not work: [1, 2, 3] and [4] have medians 2 and 4, their average is 3, while the median of the union is 2.5.
cards/9/q: You are solving Median of Two Sorted Arrays out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/9/items/0: Clarify: can an array be empty? Return a double? Are there duplicates?
cards/9/items/1: Naive: merge with two pointers up to the middle — O(m + n), while O(log(m + n)) is required
cards/9/items/2: Idea: search for the cut — i numbers from a and half − i from b — with binary search over the shorter array
cards/9/items/3: Code: the condition a[i − 1] ≤ b[j] and b[j − 1] ≤ a[i], sentinels at the edges, the array swap
cards/9/items/4: Run [1, 3] and [2]: the shorter is [2]; i = 0 is too few (3 > 2), i = 1 is correct, median max(2, 1) = 2
cards/9/items/5: Complexity: O(log min(m, n)) time, O(1) memory
cards/9/items/6: Edge cases: an empty array, an even total and dividing by 2.0, duplicates
cards/9/explain: A dry run on a tiny example is especially valuable here: it immediately shows that the sentinels work (with i = 0 the left edge of a is −∞) and that the swap is in place.
cards/10/title: Why a correct cut always exists
cards/10/body:
Monotonicity. Call i “too large” if a[i − 1] > b[j]. Increasing i by one does not decrease a[i − 1] and does not increase b[j] (j went down) — so any larger i is too large as well. “Too small” is monotonic in the other direction. So the “too small” values of i form the start of [0, m] and the “too large” ones its end. It remains to show that at least one i in between is neither. The ends: i = 0 is never too large (a[−1] = −∞), i = m is never too small (a[m] = +∞). Neighbours: if i is too small, then b[j − 1] > a[i]; for i + 1 the right edge of b is that same b[j − 1] and the left edge of a is that same a[i], and a[i] > b[j − 1] is impossible. So a “too small” i is never directly followed by a “too large” one — there is a correct cut between them, and binary search over i finds it.

The cost. There are m + 1 candidates for i, so at most ⌊log₂(m + 1)⌋ + 1 iterations, each O(1): with m = 1000 that is 10 iterations versus a thousand merge steps.
cards/10/deep:
Overflow in the average. (Math.Max(al, bl) + Math.Min(ar, br)) / 2.0 adds in int and only then divides in double. On two arrays [int.MaxValue] this formula returns −1. Under LeetCode constraints (±10⁶) it does not matter, but noticing it is a senior trait.

The k-th element by elimination. Another solution for the k-th element: compare a[k/2 − 1] and b[k/2 − 1]. The smaller one and everything to its left in its array cannot be the k-th (at most k − 2 numbers are smaller than it: k/2 − 1 from its own array and fewer than k/2 from the other), so drop those k/2 and decrease k. O(log k) = O(log(m + n)) — enough for #4, but not O(log min(m, n)).

Binary search over the value. Yet another route is binary search on the answer from the previous lesson: find the least x such that the union has at least k numbers ≤ x. The check is two upper_bounds. O(log C · (log m + log n)), where C is the value range. Slower, but it generalises to k sorted arrays and to a matrix with sorted rows and columns (Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix, #378), where the check walks the matrix as a “staircase” in O(n).

Why (m + n + 1) / 2. With an odd total the extra element goes to the left, and the median is the left maximum; one half formula covers both cases. You can put the extra one on the right instead (half = (m + n) / 2) — then for an odd total the median is the right minimum. Just don’t mix the two.
cards/11/q: Match the situation in the solution with the action.
cards/11/pairs/2/1: int.MinValue or int.MaxValue at the edge
